chapter: Paris, Lester Young, drugs, Mississippi and later sessions
title: Richfield, West Virginia: the restaurant fight
summary: In a West Virginia restaurant the owner defended serving the band, white customers started a brawl, and the musicians fought their way out and were harassed at the dance.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: I remember another incident. We were in West Virginia in some little town called Richfield, West Virginia, and we played -- we went -- we got in this town and evidently it was something of a holiday, but we were hungry so we went in this -- we asked someone there, we saw one colored man in this town and we asked him where could we eat, and he said there's a restaurant across the street. He said, that's the only place in town that you can eat. He -- the only -- while he was there he was a bricklayer or something. He was working on a new school they were building. So we went to this restaurant and the owner was very nice, so I sat down, Claude, the trombone player -- what is his name? Claude Jones sat down by me, and Walter Johnson, the drummer. He was right next to me, and the guys were all there.

So in walked about three white guys, and they didn't sit at the counter, because we were at the counter. They sat at a table right behind the counter, right,you know, not behind the counter but behind us. So we got our food and they asked the owner why did he serve these niggers before he served him -- served them, you know.
So he said, in the first place they ordered before you did, but in the interim here comes about six or seven more white guys in while we're talking, so the owner said, well in

the first place they ordered before you did. He said, but -- this white guy said, but these are niggers. This man said, well they're as good as you are. And the fight started between the white guys, you know. They hit the owner, we had to fight our way out of there, you know.

So we finally fight our way, we get out of there, we ran over to the auditorium -- it was an armory, really, but where we were working, and we got in here. So we stayed in here until time to play, and so much harrassment this night, as we were playing. Because the women were pulling at the trombonist's slide as he was sliding, they would dance by and pull at it, you know. So we said, geez, if we can just get out of here soon enough.

So when we finished playing we all packed up and we went downstairs, but we can't leave because they've got Fletcher upstairs playing the piano. They won't let him leave. So finally they let Fletcher get out of there, you know. We got in the bus and we're driving away, and the last thing I heard was these kids who'd been up to the dance hall, goodbye nigger, you know. This is why I was glad to get back, this is -- to New York.
